newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians said turning against race row MP.
newsitem.headline: Australians said turning against race row MP.

text.p: Australia's human rights commissioner said on Sunday a popular backlash was building against Pauline Hanson, the independent politician who sparked an emotional national debate on race and immigration.

Chris Sidoti told Australian television that telephone calls to his Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission had switched from being overwhelmingly supportive of Hanson to being against her by seven to one.

"I think we are getting a backlash because people are not responding (with) knee-jerk top-of-the-head reactions," Sidoti said. "People are now considering what the issues are and responding with the essential decency that I think all Australians should."

A media monitoring firm, Rehame Australia, said on Friday that talkback radio callers had also turned against Hanson since a bipartisan parliamentary motion on Wednesday which condemned racism and reaffirmed Australia's commitment to equal rights.
On Saturday, up to 2,000 people joined in an anti-racism rally in Queensland, Hanson's own state, and rally organisers said similar demonstrations would be held across the country.

The race row was sparked by Hanson's maiden parliamentary speech on September 10, in which she warned that Australia risked being swamped by Asians and called for an immediate halt to immigration to help fight joblessness.
Less than five percent of Australia's 18 million population were born in Asia.

Business leaders fear the negative publicity the row has generated in Asia -- where some newspapers have accused Prime Minister John Howard of not repudiating Hanson quickly enough -- could harm trade ties.
Tourism officials say a number of Asian tour groups have already cancelled holidays in Australia because of the row.
The government and opposition have been trying to put the row behind them. On Sunday Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron said the debate had gone on too long.
"I don't believe the Australian people are racist at all," Senator Herron told another television channel.
"There's always wackos out there, there are always people who stir things up (and) I think it's gone on long enough.
"She (Hanson) is wrong on everything that she says and the facts can be produced to show that."
Hanson has criticised government assistance to indigenous Aborigines -- Australia's most disadvantaged people -- and said it was creating a kind of apartheid.
